claims.text: Advanced ab initio techniques can be integrated with Bayesian multi-objective optimization.
The proposed framework will use finite-temperature ab initio calculations, anharmonicity, force-constant variations, and Bayesian refinement of element-specific parameters for thermal transport.
The framework will separately model lattice vibrations and electronic transport or scattering.
The proposed approach will reduce lattice-thermal-conductivity prediction error by at least 20% relative to existing analytical models.
The target material is homogeneous, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr with minimal contamination.
HfNbTaTiZr is commonly prepared by arc melting.
The relevant HfNbTaTiZr composition is equiatomic.
Atomic-scale force-constant variations and anharmonic effects modulate lattice vibrations independently of electronic transport channels.
First-principles vibrational spectra and anharmonic scattering rates, combined with Bayesian parameter adjustment, can isolate the phonon contribution without using an averaged Debye temperature.
Separating lattice and electronic contributions will improve lattice-conductivity accuracy relative to models that merge the two contributions.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
Below 200 K, the phonon spectrum and anharmonicity dominate thermal transport.
At 300–1200 K, separated predictions will reveal the effect of approximately 1 wt.% oxygen on electronic thermal transport.
Prior analytical and DFT-based thermal-transport models use Debye temperatures or elastic properties, assume perfect bulk crystals, and conflate lattice and electronic conduction.
The proposed approach is applicable to high-purity, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr below 200 K but may require recalibration for polycrystalline or oxygen-contaminated samples above 300 K.
Thermoreflectance combined with electrical-transport measurements can independently determine the lattice thermal conductivity needed for model validation.
Failure to achieve at least a 20% relative error reduction below 200 K, or failure of the predicted contribution separation in controlled high-temperature tests, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The specimen is described as homogeneous and defect-free while dendritic microstructure is given as an example; a dendritic solidification structure generally implies spatial microstructural or compositional heterogeneity.

The hypothesis says lattice and electronic contributions are comparable below 200 K, but also treats this regime as one where phonons and anharmonicity dominate and where low temperature itself helps isolate lattice transport.

High-temperature oxygen-containing samples are proposed as a test of separated predictions, while the stated applicability boundary says oxygen-contaminated samples above 300 K may require recalibration, leaving the decisive status of that comparison ambiguous.
